title: Prototype systems for rechargeable magnesium batteries
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: An electrolyte for a magnesium-metal battery must supply species that can release or rearrange their ligands, accept electrons and join the metal. It must sustain this reaction as the surface changes. The early rechargeable prototype combined an organohaloaluminate electrolyte with a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1,2,3] Later work showed how strongly deposition depends on both the liquid and the exposed surface.[4,5] Electrolyte chemistry remains a central constraint on magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6,7,8,9] We see the next task as explaining how a working formulation delivers magnesium, so that its molecular advantage can guide the design of another formulation.

title: Nonaqueous Liquid Electrolytes for Lithium-Based Rechargeable Batteries
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: Lithium offers useful comparisons, but its familiar interphase logic needs to be reconsidered for magnesium. In many lithium electrolytes, anion participation and lower free-solvent activity help select the compounds that are reduced.[10,11,12] Concentrated formulations also change reaction selectivity and electrode compatibility.[13,14,15] A useful lithium interphase limits electron leakage while allowing ionic transport.[16,17] Similar surface products do not establish similar magnesium transport. Magnesium films often block transfer, although designed interphases can sustain cycling.[18,19,20] The design criterion is a functioning interface under the intended conditions; borrowing a favourable lithium film composition is insufficient.

title: Organic Electrolyte Design for Rechargeable Batteries: From Lithium to Magnesium
section: 1.1. Why magnesium needs its own electrolyte logic
text: The distinction begins with Mg²⁺. Its higher charge generally strengthens binding to comparable donors relative to Li⁺; denticity, ion association and polarization then reshape the shell.[21,22] Removing a donor changes the environment of those that remain. Binding an anion changes the charge and geometry of the complex, sometimes opening a different release route. The reacting species may therefore differ from the dominant bulk solvate. The apparent paradox follows: lithium-inspired reasoning encourages anion participation for film formation, whereas strong-binding reasoning encourages anion exclusion to ease release. Both directions have produced working magnesium electrolytes.[23,24] Understanding which reaction they improve resolves this contradiction.

section: 1.2. A working recipe needs a reaction mechanism
text: A successful recipe is not yet an explanation. Magnesium electrolyte development spans several salt and solvent families,[25,26,27,28] but changing a solvent changes dissolution, ion pairing, exchange and surface reactions together. A lower overpotential can reflect any of these effects. Donor number, mean coordination number and isolated binding energy describe parts of the liquid; none identifies the slow reaction by itself. Calculations already connect magnesium coordination with pairing and decomposition.[22,29,30] The priority is a prediction about a defined transfer step that can guide a composition change.

title: Solvent–Anion Counterpoised Electrolyte Enables High‐Rate Magnesium Metal Batteries
section: 1.3. Our position and the criterion for progress
text: We propose choosing a first-shell anion for its effect on magnesium transfer. Coordination can replace a persistent solvent donor, redistribute charge and alter how the remaining ligands depart as the complex approaches the electrode. Anion–solvent interactions can also make a reactive precursor more accessible. These changes act on the sequence leading to reduction, whether or not the anion later forms a film. Counterpoised interactions, dynamic solvation and regulation beyond the primary shell provide current examples of this reasoning.[24,37,38] Treating anions mainly as SEI precursors misses this earlier molecular role. The important test is whether the change enables selective metal transfer.

title: A weakly ion pairing electrolyte designed for high voltage magnesium batteries
section: 2.1. Weak pairing avoids an unproductive association
text: Weak pairing helps when association creates a precursor that exchanges slowly or reacts unfavourably. A solvent-designed Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte shows that promoting ion-pair dissociation can support deposition and a high-voltage cathode.[23] Earlier TFSI studies also show that the donor environment and cycling history change the response at magnesium.[39,40,41] Weak pairing removes a particular obstacle. The remaining solvent shell still has to rearrange and avoid reduction. High dissociation and high conductivity are therefore useful observations, but they do not establish an accessible metal-transfer reaction.
